Jerusalem.desc: Holy city on the Judean plateau; capital of united Israel under David and Solomon, site of the Temple, and the spiritual center of Jewish faith for a millennium.

events.text: Melchizedek, king of Salem (Jerusalem), brings out bread and wine to bless Abram after his victory — the first priest-king foreshadowing Christ.
Abraham offers Isaac on Mount Moriah, the very ridge where Solomon will build the Temple and where the Lamb of God will be crucified.
David captures the Jebusite stronghold and makes it his royal capital, naming it the City of David.
Solomon builds the First Temple on Mount Moriah over seven years — a structure housing the Ark of the Covenant and God's manifest glory.
Nebuchadnezzar's forces breach the walls, burn the Temple, and exile the population to Babylon in 586 BC, ending the monarchy.
Nehemiah surveys the shattered walls at night, then rallies the returned exiles to rebuild them in a remarkable 52 days.
'I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD.' The great pilgrimage psalm celebrates Jerusalem as the throne of David and goal of worship.
Isaiah envisions all nations streaming to Mount Zion in the latter days to receive God's instruction and to end war.
Jesus enters on a donkey to shouts of 'Hosanna!' — fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 and setting in motion the events of Passion Week.
The Holy Spirit descends at Pentecost, and 3,000 are baptized. Jerusalem becomes the birthplace of the church.
The New Jerusalem descends from heaven, radiant as a bride. God dwells with his people permanently — the city of pure light.

Bethlehem.region: Judean highlands, 8 km S of Jerusalem
Bethlehem.desc: Small town in Judah famous as the hometown of Ruth and Boaz, the birthplace of David, and the prophesied birthplace of the Messiah.

events.text: Naomi returns to Bethlehem from Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth, arriving at barley harvest — the opening scene of Israel's great redemption story.
Boaz redeems Ruth in Bethlehem's gate; they marry and become great-grandparents of David.
Samuel comes to Bethlehem and secretly anoints the shepherd boy David as Israel's future king.
David leaves Bethlehem to bring food to his brothers at the Valley of Elah, where he will kill Goliath.
'But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah... from you shall come forth one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origin is from of old.' The Messiah prophecy.
Jesus is born in Bethlehem, fulfilling Micah 5:2. Magi follow a star; Herod massacres the infants in a futile attempt to destroy the child-king.
Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem for the census. Jesus is born in a manger, and shepherds hear the angelic announcement.

Nazareth.desc: Small hillside village in Galilee where Jesus grew up — so obscure that Nathanael quipped, 'Can anything good come from Nazareth?'

events.text: The angel Gabriel appears to Mary in Nazareth to announce that she will conceive the Son of God.
Joseph and Mary return to Nazareth after the birth and Egyptian sojourn. Jesus grows up there in wisdom and stature.
Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and declares, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.' The crowd then tries to throw him off a cliff.
Nathanael's skeptical question — 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?' — is answered when he meets Jesus and declares him the Son of God.
The family settles in Nazareth after returning from Egypt, fulfilling the prophecy 'He shall be called a Nazarene.'

Capernaum.region: NW shore of the Sea of Galilee
Capernaum.desc: Fishing town on the Sea of Galilee that became Jesus's ministry headquarters — site of more miracles than anywhere else, yet condemned for its unbelief.

events.text: Jesus leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah 9:1-2 — 'the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light.'
In Capernaum's synagogue Jesus casts out an unclean spirit, and the crowd marvels at his authority. He then heals Peter's mother-in-law.
Friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof of the house where Jesus is teaching. Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.
After feeding 5,000 near Capernaum, Jesus delivers the 'Bread of Life' discourse in the synagogue. Many disciples turn back.
Jesus pronounces woe on Capernaum: 'You will be brought down to Hades' — because it saw the most miracles yet did not repent.
Jesus pays the temple tax from a coin found in a fish's mouth, miraculously provided in Capernaum.

Jericho.region: Jordan Valley, just W of Jordan River
Jericho.desc: The oldest continuously inhabited city on earth, guarding the entry to Canaan from the east. Its fall opened the conquest; its healing of Bartimaeus opened Jesus's final journey to Jerusalem.

events.text: Joshua sends two spies to Jericho. Rahab hides them and is promised salvation for her household — a scarlet cord in her window.
Israel marches around Jericho for seven days. The walls collapse at the trumpet blast and the shout of the people. Only Rahab's house stands.
Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho, losing two sons in the process — fulfilling Joshua's curse spoken five centuries earlier.
Elisha purifies Jericho's bitter water by throwing salt into the spring, making it wholesome to this day.
Jesus sets his parable of the Good Samaritan on the Jericho road — the dangerous descent where a priest and Levite pass by the wounded man.
Blind Bartimaeus calls out 'Son of David, have mercy on me!' near Jericho. Jesus heals him, and he follows on the road to Jerusalem.
Zacchaeus the tax collector climbs a sycamore tree in Jericho to see Jesus, who invites himself to his house. Salvation comes to Zacchaeus's house.

Hebron.region: Judean highlands, 30 km S of Jerusalem
Hebron.desc: Ancient city in the hills of Judah where Abraham settled and was buried. David's first capital before capturing Jerusalem.

events.text: Abram settles near Hebron at Mamre's oaks and builds an altar to the LORD after separating from Lot.
Three visitors (including the LORD) appear to Abraham at Mamre/Hebron. Sarah laughs at the promise of a son in her old age.
Sarah dies at Hebron. Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah as the family burial ground — the first piece of the Promised Land he owns.
Caleb claims Hebron as his inheritance, 45 years after spying the land, saying he is still as strong as when Moses sent him.
After Saul's death, David is anointed king over Judah in Hebron, where he reigns for seven and a half years before taking Jerusalem.
Absalom launches his rebellion from Hebron, where he was born and where his political grievances had long festered.

Bethel.region: Central highlands, 18 km N of Jerusalem
Bethel.desc: Sacred site where Abraham built an altar, Jacob saw the stairway to heaven, and the ark temporarily rested. Later became a center of false worship under Jeroboam.

events.text: Abram builds his second altar near Bethel after arriving in Canaan, calling on the name of the LORD.
Jacob flees to Haran and dreams at this spot of a stairway reaching heaven, with angels ascending and descending. He names it Bethel — 'House of God.'
God appears to Jacob at Bethel again, renaming him Israel and renewing the covenant promises of land and descendants.
The tribes of Israel gather at Bethel to inquire of God about the war against Benjamin over the Gibeah atrocity.
Jeroboam sets up a golden calf at Bethel, declaring 'Here are your gods, O Israel.' It becomes a major center of syncretism throughout the Northern Kingdom.
The prophet Amos preaches judgment against the Bethel sanctuary; the priest Amaziah orders him to leave the country.

Shechem.region: Between Mounts Gerizim and Ebal, central Canaan
Shechem.desc: Strategic city in central Canaan between two mountains. The first place Abram stopped; where the nation renewed the covenant; scene of Joseph's search for his brothers.

events.text: Abram stops at Shechem at the oak of Moreh — the first place in Canaan where God promises the land to his offspring.
Dinah, Jacob's daughter, is violated by Shechem the prince. Her brothers Simeon and Levi massacre the city in revenge.
Jacob sends Joseph from Hebron to check on his brothers at Shechem; he is sold into slavery at Dothan nearby.
Joshua assembles all Israel at Shechem for a covenant renewal ceremony: 'Choose this day whom you will serve.'
Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be crowned, but his harsh answer splits the kingdom. Jeroboam makes Shechem his first capital.
At Jacob's Well near Sychar (ancient Shechem), Jesus offers a Samaritan woman 'living water' — the longest one-on-one conversation in the Gospels.

Shiloh.desc: Location of the Tabernacle and the Ark of the Covenant for roughly 300 years during the period of the judges. Samuel grew up here.

events.text: The whole Israelite assembly gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tabernacle after the initial conquest. The remaining land is divided there.
The tribes gather at Shiloh to grieve the near-extinction of Benjamin and arrange for wives for the survivors.
Hannah prays in anguish at the Shiloh sanctuary for a son, making a vow. The priest Eli blesses her; she conceives Samuel.
The boy Samuel, serving Eli at Shiloh, hears God call his name three times. God's word is rare in those days; Samuel becomes his prophet.
The Ark of the Covenant is taken from Shiloh to battle against the Philistines, who capture it. Eli dies upon hearing the news.
Psalm 78 recalls how God 'abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh' as a warning against hardening the heart — the sanctuary's destruction as a sign of judgment.
Jeremiah warns Jerusalem that God will do to the Temple what he did to Shiloh — destroy it utterly — unless the people repent.

Beersheba.desc: The southernmost city of the Promised Land, marking the boundary 'from Dan to Beersheba.' Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all encountered God here.

events.text: Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant at Beersheba over a well — the city's name means 'Well of the Oath' or 'Well of Seven.'
Abraham departs from Beersheba for Moriah to offer Isaac, returning here after God provides the ram.
God appears to Isaac at Beersheba with the covenant promise; Isaac builds an altar there. Abimelech makes another treaty here.
Jacob stops at Beersheba as he journeys to Egypt; God reassures him in a night vision: 'Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt.'
Elijah flees from Jezebel to Beersheba, leaves his servant there, and walks a day into the wilderness — exhausted and ready to die — before an angel feeds him.
Amos twice warns Israel not to seek God at Beersheba, as their pilgrimages there have become empty religion disconnected from justice.

Gilgal.desc: Israel's first camp in Canaan after crossing the Jordan, where circumcision was renewed and the Passover first celebrated in the land. Samuel's circuit court and the place Saul was crowned.

events.text: Twelve stones are set up at Gilgal, taken from the Jordan riverbed, as a permanent memorial of the miraculous crossing.
God commands Israel to circumcise all males at Gilgal — rolling away 'the reproach of Egypt.' They celebrate the first Passover in Canaan here.
After Saul's victory over the Ammonites, Samuel renews the kingdom at Gilgal and all Israel rejoices and sacrifices before the LORD.
Saul unlawfully offers the burnt offering at Gilgal without waiting for Samuel. Samuel pronounces that his kingdom will not endure.
Hosea condemns Israel's wickedness at Gilgal: 'All their evil is at Gilgal; there I began to hate them.' The sacred site has become a place of sin.

Egypt.desc: The great ancient superpower where Israel was enslaved for 430 years. From famine refuge to house of bondage to the arena of God's greatest pre-Christ redemptive act.

events.text: Abram goes to Egypt during a famine. Pharaoh takes Sarai, but God plagues Pharaoh's house until she is returned.
Joseph is sold to Ishmaelite traders who take him to Egypt, where he will rise from slave to second-in-command.
Jacob's entire family — 70 persons — descends to Egypt at Pharaoh's invitation and settles in the land of Goshen.
A new Pharaoh who did not know Joseph enslaves Israel and orders the murder of newborn Hebrew boys.
The tenth plague kills Egypt's firstborn; Israel is spared by the Passover blood. Pharaoh expels the Hebrews in the night.
Joseph flees with Mary and the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre, fulfilling 'Out of Egypt I called my son' (Hosea 11:1).
The great city where the two witnesses are killed is symbolically called 'Sodom and Egypt' — representing spiritual oppression and worldly bondage.

Babylon.desc: The great empire that destroyed Jerusalem, burned the Temple, and exiled Judah. In Scripture, Babylon becomes the symbol of all arrogant human empire set against God.

events.text: At Babel (Babylon), humanity builds a tower to reach heaven. God confuses the languages and scatters the people — pride becomes the foundation of division.
Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and takes the first exiles to Babylon, including Jehoiachin and the young nobles.
Nebuchadnezzar destroys Solomon's Temple and deports virtually the entire population of Judah to Babylon in 586 BC.
Daniel and his three friends are taken to Babylon's royal court. They refuse the king's food and God grants them superior wisdom.
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are thrown into Babylon's furnace for refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar's golden image. A fourth figure walks with them.
'By the waters of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion.' The haunting psalm of exile and longing.
Isaiah pronounces the fall of Babylon centuries in advance: 'Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon.'
'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!' — the apocalyptic city symbolizing all worldly power, luxury, and persecution of God's people, brought to ruin in an hour.

Nineveh.desc: Capital of the Assyrian Empire — Israel's most feared enemy. The city that repented at Jonah's preaching, and that later destroyed the Northern Kingdom.

events.text: Nineveh is built by Nimrod after the flood — described as 'a great city.' It will become the most powerful city in the ancient world.
God commands Jonah to preach to Nineveh. Jonah flees by ship to Tarshish instead, is swallowed by a great fish, and spends three days in its belly.
Jonah preaches in Nineveh and the entire city — from the king to the cattle — repents in sackcloth and ash. God relents from the disaster.
Jonah is angry at God's mercy to Nineveh. God uses a withered plant to teach him about compassion for 120,000 people who don't know their right hand from their left.
The Assyrian king Sennacherib threatens Jerusalem from Nineveh. God strikes down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in the night; Sennacherib is later murdered by his own sons.
Nahum prophesies the total destruction of Nineveh over a century after Jonah's revival: 'Woe to the bloody city!' Nineveh falls to Babylon in 612 BC.

Jesus cites the people of Nineveh as a rebuke to his generation: 'The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment... for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.'

Sinai.desc: The holy mountain where God revealed himself in fire and gave Moses the Ten Commandments. The site of Israel's covenant with God — the defining event of the nation's history.

events.text: Moses encounters the burning bush at Horeb (Sinai) and receives his commission: God reveals his name 'I AM WHO I AM' and sends Moses to deliver Israel.
Israel camps at the base of Sinai. The mountain thunders, blazes with fire, and shakes. God descends in cloud and speaks the Ten Commandments.
Moses ascends the mountain into the cloud of God's glory for 40 days to receive the full law and the pattern for the Tabernacle.
While Moses is on the mountain, Israel makes and worships the golden calf. Moses shatters the tablets of the covenant at the base.
God renews the covenant and allows Moses to see his glory — his back — passing by. Moses descends with a radiant face.
Elijah flees Jezebel and travels 40 days to Horeb. God speaks not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in 'a still, small voice' — and recommissions the exhausted prophet.
Paul uses Sinai (Hagar) as a symbol of the old covenant of law and slavery, contrasted with Jerusalem above (Sarah) — the covenant of promise and freedom.

Jordan.region: Rift valley from Sea of Galilee to Dead Sea
Jordan.desc: The great river marking the eastern boundary of the Promised Land. Crossed miraculously by Israel under Joshua, by Elijah and Elisha, and the site of Jesus's baptism.

events.text: Lot sees the whole plain of the Jordan is well watered 'like the garden of the LORD' and chooses it for himself, pitching his tent near Sodom.
The priests carrying the Ark step into the Jordan at flood stage; the waters pile up and Israel crosses on dry ground — a second Exodus.
Elijah strikes the Jordan with his cloak and the waters part for him and Elisha to cross. Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind; Elisha parts the river again on his return.
Naaman the Syrian general is instructed to dip seven times in the Jordan to be healed of leprosy. He angrily objects to the ordinary river, then obeys and is cleansed.
John baptizes in the Jordan at Bethany-beyond-the-Jordan. Jesus is baptized; the Spirit descends as a dove and the Father's voice declares, 'This is my beloved Son.'
John the Baptist testifies about Jesus from the Jordan: 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!'

Galilee.desc: The northern region of Israel, home to most of Jesus's ministry. The Sea of Galilee — a freshwater lake — was the workplace of several apostles and the stage of some of Jesus's most dramatic miracles.

events.text: Isaiah prophesied that 'Galilee of the Gentiles' would see a great light — fulfilled when Jesus made Capernaum his base.
Jesus calls his first disciples by the Sea of Galilee: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.' Peter, Andrew, James, and John leave their nets.
Jesus walks on the Sea of Galilee in a storm. Peter steps out and begins to sink; Jesus catches him — 'You of little faith, why did you doubt?'
After a night of failed fishing, Peter lets down the nets at Jesus's word. The catch breaks the nets. Peter falls to his knees: 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.'
Jesus feeds 5,000 people on the NE shore of the Sea of Galilee with five loaves and two fish, then sends the crowd away and crosses the lake on foot.
The risen Jesus appears to seven disciples fishing on the Sea of Galilee, cooks breakfast on the shore, and reinstates Peter with three questions of love.

Samaria.region: Central Israel, between Galilee and Judea
Samaria.desc: Capital of the Northern Kingdom built by Omri on a hill he purchased. The region later inhabited by a mixed population whose worship scandalized the Jews.

events.text: Omri buys the hill of Samaria and builds his capital there, naming it after its original owner Shemer. His son Ahab rules here.
Elijah confronts Ahab in Samaria and challenges the Baal prophets to a contest on Mount Carmel. The city has become a center of Baal worship.
Ben-hadad's army besieges Samaria, causing famine. God causes the Aramean army to flee in the night, and Samaria is saved.
The Assyrians under Sargon II conquer Samaria and deport its people in 722 BC, ending the Northern Kingdom. Foreign peoples are resettled there.
Jesus travels through Samaria and stops at Jacob's Well in Sychar. His conversation with the Samaritan woman — five husbands, living water — leads the whole town to believe.
After Stephen's martyrdom, Philip preaches in Samaria. The city receives the word with joy and miracles; Peter and John come down to pray for the Samaritan believers.

Tyre.desc: Great Phoenician port city, fabulously wealthy from maritime trade. Israel's ally under David and Solomon; later a target of prophetic judgment.

events.text: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar wood and craftsmen to build David's palace — the beginning of a lasting alliance between Israel and Phoenicia.
Solomon contracts with Hiram of Tyre for cedar and cypress lumber for the Temple, paying in wheat and oil. Thousands of laborers work the project.
Ezekiel delivers a stunning oracle against Tyre, describing in detail how Nebuchadnezzar will besiege it and Alexander will later scrape its rubble into the sea.
The lament over the king of Tyre contains imagery of a glorious being in Eden, often interpreted as a description of Satan's original state and fall.
Jesus declares that even Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen his miracles — unlike Chorazin and Bethsaida who witnessed them and did not.
Paul stops in Tyre for a week on his way to Jerusalem. The disciples there, through the Spirit, urge him not to go — but Paul continues to Jerusalem and his arrest.

Damascus.desc: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities; capital of Aram (Syria) and Israel's frequent enemy and sometimes ally. The road to Damascus transformed the church's greatest missionary.

events.text: Abram pursues the kings who took Lot captive all the way to Dan and Hobah, near Damascus — an extraordinary 300-mile rescue mission.
Abram's chief servant Eliezer is 'of Damascus' — the man he trusts to find a wife for Isaac.
David defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and garrisons Damascus, making it a vassal state and bringing tribute to Jerusalem.
God commands Elijah to anoint Hazael as king over Syria (Damascus) — the foreign rod of discipline God will use against Israel.
Amos opens his oracle collection with the judgment of Damascus: 'For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment.'
Saul of Tarsus, on the road to Damascus to persecute Christians, is blinded by a light from heaven and hears Jesus's voice. He is baptized in Damascus and begins preaching Christ.

Ur.desc: Sophisticated Sumerian city-state on the Euphrates where Abraham was born and from which God called him on his foundational journey of faith.

events.text: Terah takes Abram, Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan. They settle in Haran instead.
God identifies himself to Abram: 'I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land.'
In Israel's great confessional prayer, they recall: 'You are the LORD God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans.'
Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrin begins with God appearing to Abraham 'in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran' — an original act of grace before any obedience.
'By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.' — Ur to Canaan.

Haran.desc: Trading city on the Balikh River where Terah settled and died; the family home to which Jacob fled and where he lived twenty years, marrying Leah and Rachel.

events.text: Terah sets out for Canaan with his family but stops and settles in Haran, where he dies at age 205.
After Terah dies, God calls Abram to leave Haran for the land he will show him. Abram departs at 75 years old.
Rebekah urges Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran to escape Esau's wrath after stealing the blessing. Isaac sends him to find a wife there.
Jacob arrives in Haran and meets Rachel at a well. He works seven years for her, but Laban tricks him into marrying Leah first. He works another seven years for Rachel.
After twenty years, Jacob secretly leaves Haran with his family and flocks. Laban pursues and catches him; they make a covenant at Mizpah.

Midian.region: NW Arabia, E of the Gulf of Aqaba
Midian.desc: Desert territory east of Sinai inhabited by Abraham's descendants through Keturah. Moses spent 40 years here after fleeing Egypt; Jethro (his father-in-law) was a Midianite priest.

events.text: The Midianite traders who pass through Dothan buy Joseph from his brothers for 20 shekels of silver and take him to Egypt.
Moses flees Egypt after killing an Egyptian taskmaster and settles in Midian. He marries Zipporah, daughter of Jethro the priest.
While tending Jethro's flocks in Midian near Horeb, Moses sees the burning bush and receives his commission to deliver Israel.
Jethro (Moses's Midianite father-in-law) hears of the Exodus, comes to meet Moses, and advises him to appoint judges — wise management counsel.
God commands Israel to execute judgment on Midian for the Baal Peor seduction that killed 24,000 Israelites. Five Midianite kings are killed.
Gideon defeats an overwhelming Midianite army of 135,000 with only 300 men armed with trumpets and torches — one of the Bible's most dramatic military stories.

Mount Carmel.desc: Forested coastal mountain that juts into the Mediterranean. Site of Elijah's great showdown with the 450 prophets of Baal — the decisive moment for Israelite monotheism.

events.text: Elijah challenges 450 Baal prophets and 400 Asherah prophets on Carmel. After hours of futile ritual, Elijah prays simply — and fire falls from heaven and consumes the offering and altar.
After three and a half years of drought, Elijah climbs to the top of Carmel, prays seven times, and the rains return. He outruns Ahab's chariot to Jezreel.
Elisha returns to Carmel after watching Elijah taken up to heaven. His ministry begins with authority on the same mountain where Elijah's great victory occurred.
'Your head crowns you like Carmel' — the beloved's beauty is compared to the magnificent wooded mountain, its richness and majesty.
Isaiah promises Israel that the glory and majesty of Carmel and Sharon will be given to them — a symbol of God's lavish blessing on his restored people.

Mount of Olives.region: E of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley
Mount of Olives.desc: The ridge immediately east of Jerusalem, separated by the Kidron Valley. Site of David's flight, Ezekiel's vision of God's departure, Jesus's great discourse, his agony, and the promised site of his return.

events.text: David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping and barefoot when he flees Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion — a king in tears foreshadowing Jesus's own ascent.
Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD leave the Jerusalem Temple and stand on the mountain east of the city — the Mount of Olives — before departing entirely.
Zechariah prophesies that the LORD will stand on the Mount of Olives in the last day, and the mountain will split in two to provide an escape route.
Sitting on the Mount of Olives, Jesus delivers his great Olivet Discourse — signs of the end, the fall of Jerusalem, and his return in glory.
Jesus prays in Gethsemane (at the foot of the Mount of Olives): 'Not my will but yours be done.' He is arrested here.
Jesus ascends to heaven from the Mount of Olives. Two angels declare: 'This same Jesus... will come back in the same way you have seen him go into heaven.'

Gethsemane.region: Foot of the Mount of Olives, E Jerusalem
Gethsemane.desc: An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives where Jesus often withdrew with his disciples. The scene of his most intense prayer and his arrest.

events.text: Jesus falls on his face and prays, 'My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.' Three times. The disciples sleep.
Luke records that Jesus's sweat fell like drops of blood as he prayed — a physiological sign of extreme distress. An angel from heaven strengthens him.
John emphasizes that Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley to the garden, fulfilling his role as the true Passover lamb. Jesus steps forward to identify himself and the soldiers fall to the ground.
Judas arrives with a crowd of soldiers and betrays Jesus with a kiss. Peter draws his sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus heals the ear.
When Jesus says 'I am he,' the soldiers and officers fall backward to the ground — a final demonstration of his divine authority before yielding to arrest.

Golgotha.desc: The hill outside Jerusalem's walls where Jesus was crucified. The name in Aramaic and Latin means 'Place of the Skull.' The pivotal location of human history.

events.text: Jesus is led to Golgotha and crucified between two criminals. From noon to three the whole land is dark; then Jesus cries out and gives up his spirit.
At Golgotha Jesus prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' He promises paradise to the repentant thief beside him.
John is an eyewitness: the title 'King of the Jews' is posted in three languages; soldiers divide his garments; Jesus commits his mother to John's care; 'It is finished.'
When Jesus dies, the Temple curtain tears in two from top to bottom. The centurion standing opposite says, 'Truly this man was the Son of God.'

Bethany.region: E slope of Mount of Olives / beyond Jordan
Bethany.desc: A village just 3 km from Jerusalem where Jesus's dear friends Mary, Martha, and Lazarus lived — a place of refuge, weeping, and resurrection.

events.text: Jesus visits Mary and Martha in Bethany. Martha is busy serving; Mary sits at Jesus's feet. Jesus says Mary has chosen 'the one thing necessary.'
Lazarus, Jesus's friend, dies in Bethany. Jesus arrives four days later, weeps at the tomb, and calls Lazarus out alive — the seventh and greatest sign in John.
Six days before Passover, a dinner in Bethany. Mary anoints Jesus's feet with a pound of expensive nard. Judas objects; Jesus says she has prepared him for burial.
Jesus leads his disciples to the vicinity of Bethany and ascends to heaven there, blessing them as he goes.

Joppa.region: Mediterranean coast, modern Tel Aviv area
Joppa.desc: The ancient Mediterranean port of Jerusalem — Israel's primary gateway to the sea. A city of reluctant prophets and restored life.

events.text: Cedar logs from Lebanon for Solomon's Temple are floated by raft down the coast to Joppa, then carried overland up to Jerusalem.
Jonah goes to Joppa to find a ship sailing to Tarshish — a direct flight in the opposite direction from God's commission.
Cedar trees from Lebanon are again brought by sea to Joppa for the rebuilding of the Second Temple under Zerubbabel.
Peter is summoned to Joppa, where Tabitha (Dorcas) has died. He prays and she opens her eyes — a resurrection that brings many to believe.
While staying in Joppa at the house of Simon the tanner, Peter receives a vision of a sheet of unclean animals: 'What God has made clean, do not call common.' Cornelius's messengers arrive.

Caesarea.desc: Herod's magnificent port city built with an artificial harbor. The Roman administrative capital of Judea and scene of pivotal moments in Acts.

events.text: Philip the evangelist, after preaching across Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch on the Gaza road, ends up at Caesarea and settles there.
Cornelius, a Roman centurion in Caesarea, has a vision directing him to send for Peter. Peter comes, preaches, and the Holy Spirit falls on Gentiles for the first time.
Herod Agrippa delivers a speech in Caesarea and the crowd shouts 'The voice of a god!' An angel strikes him and he is eaten by worms.
Paul stops in Caesarea at Philip's house. The prophet Agabus binds Paul's hands with his belt, foretelling his arrest in Jerusalem.
Paul stands before Festus in Caesarea and appeals to Caesar. King Agrippa II hears Paul's defense: 'In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian.'

Caesarea Philippi.region: Base of Mount Hermon, N Israel
Caesarea Philippi.desc: A Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon near the headwaters of the Jordan, built by Philip the tetrarch. The backdrop for Peter's great confession.

events.text: The tribe of Dan conquers the city of Laish at the foot of Hermon and renames it Dan — the northernmost city of Israel.
Jeroboam places one of his golden calves at Dan, the northern boundary of his kingdom, to prevent pilgrims from going to Jerusalem.

At Caesarea Philippi, against the backdrop of pagan temples, Jesus asks 'Who do you say that I am?' Peter answers: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' Jesus declares he will build his church.
Jesus rebukes Peter sharply here when Peter protests the coming suffering: 'Get behind me, Satan! You are not setting your mind on the things of God.'

Antioch.desc: Third largest city of the Roman Empire; the birthplace of the name 'Christians' and the launching base for Paul's three missionary journeys.

events.text: Believers scattered by Stephen's persecution reach Antioch and begin preaching to Greeks. 'In Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.'
The Holy Spirit says to the Antioch church: 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' The first missionary journey begins.
Paul and Barnabas return to Antioch after the first journey and report all that God has done — the church's first missionary debrief.
The Jerusalem Council debates circumcision. Paul and Barnabas carry the council's letter back to Antioch, releasing the Gentile believers from the law.
Paul publicly opposes Peter in Antioch when Peter withdraws from eating with Gentiles under pressure from Jerusalem — a key moment defining justification by faith.

Corinth.region: Greece, isthmus between N and S Greece
Corinth.desc: The commercial capital of Greece, notorious for its wealth, immorality, and diversity. Paul planted a church here that became one of the most problematic and instructed in the NT.

events.text: Paul arrives in Corinth, meets Priscilla and Aquila (tentmakers like him), and stays 18 months — his longest stay in any city on the missionary journeys.
God speaks to Paul in Corinth at night: 'Do not be afraid... I have many people in this city.' Paul continues boldly despite opposition.
Paul writes to address deep divisions in the Corinthian church — factions, lawsuits, sexual immorality — and grounds everything in the foolishness of the cross.
The great resurrection chapter is written to Corinth: '...if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.' Paul lists resurrection appearances.
Paul defends his apostleship against 'super apostles' in Corinth with an extraordinary catalogue of sufferings: shipwrecks, beatings, sleepless nights, burden for all the churches.

Athens.desc: Cultural and intellectual capital of the Greek world. Paul's sermon at the Areopagus is the model for engaging pagan philosophy with the gospel.

events.text: Paul's spirit is provoked by Athens's idols. He reasons daily in the synagogue and agora. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus.
On the Areopagus, Paul delivers a masterclass in contextualization: 'Men of Athens... the unknown God whom you worship I now proclaim to you.'
The resurrection divides the crowd: some mock, some want to hear more, some believe — including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.
Paul writes from Athens that he 'could bear it no longer' and sent Timothy to strengthen the Thessalonian church while he waited alone in Athens.

Ephesus.desc: One of the largest cities in the Roman Empire, home of the temple of Artemis (one of the Seven Wonders). Paul's longest ministry stay — three years — and the base for spreading the gospel across Asia.

events.text: Apollos, an eloquent man mighty in the Scriptures, arrives in Ephesus knowing only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila explain the way of God more accurately.
Paul spends two years in the lecture hall of Tyrannus; 'all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord.' Extraordinary miracles follow.
The silversmiths' riot: Demetrius rallies craftsmen against Paul because the gospel is destroying the trade in Artemis shrines — 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!'
Paul bids farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, warning of coming wolves. His longest farewell speech in Acts.
Paul's letter to Ephesus describes the church as Christ's body, chosen before creation, sealed by the Spirit, and raised together with Christ.
The risen Christ commends Ephesus for endurance and discernment but rebukes them: 'You have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen.'

Rome.desc: Capital of the empire that crucified Jesus, persecuted the church, and eventually became Christian. Paul's letter to Rome is the fullest exposition of the gospel in the NT.

events.text: Claudius expels all Jews from Rome; Priscilla and Aquila leave Rome and meet Paul in Corinth — Rome's expelled Jews becoming the gospel's ambassadors.
After the Ephesus riot, Paul resolves 'I must also see Rome' — his destination for 3 more chapters of Acts and years of imprisonment.
Paul's voyage to Rome includes the great shipwreck off Malta. He arrives in Rome under house arrest and 'welcomed all who came to him' for two years.
Paul writes to Rome: 'I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.' He addresses a church he has never visited.
The great chapter of assurance — 'no condemnation... the Spirit intercedes for us... nothing can separate us from the love of God' — written from Corinth to Rome.
'Babylon the great' seated on seven hills, drunk with the blood of the saints — most scholars see this as Rome, the persecuting empire of John's day.

Philippi.desc: A leading Roman colony in Macedonia. Paul's first European church, marked from the beginning by a businesswoman, a slave girl, an earthquake, and a jailer's baptism.

events.text: Paul's Macedonian vision ('Come over and help us') brings him to Philippi. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, is the first European convert. Her household is baptized.
Paul exorcises a spirit of divination from a slave girl. Her owners have Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. At midnight they sing hymns — a great earthquake opens the prison.
The jailer, terrified, asks 'What must I do to be saved?' Paul: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved.' The jailer and his household are baptized.
Paul writes to Philippi from prison: 'I thank my God in all my remembrance of you... I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion.'
'Rejoice in the Lord always... The Lord is at hand... I can do all things through him who strengthens me.' Paul's joy-letter from chains.

Thessalonica.desc: Capital of the Roman province of Macedonia. Paul preached here for only a few weeks but left a church committed to the gospel — facing severe persecution and eagerly awaiting Christ's return.

events.text: Paul reasons three Sabbaths in Thessalonica's synagogue from the Scriptures: 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.' A violent mob chases him out.
The mob accuses the Thessalonian believers before the city authorities: 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also.'
Paul addresses their grief about believers who died: 'We who are alive... will be caught up together with them... And so we will always be with the Lord.'
Paul corrects a false teaching that the day of the Lord has already come, explaining the apostasy and the man of lawlessness must come first.

Patmos.desc: Small rocky island in the Aegean where the apostle John was exiled 'for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.' There he received the Revelation.

events.text: 'I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation... was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.'
On the Lord's Day on Patmos, John hears a trumpet-like voice and turns to see the glorified Christ — hair white as wool, eyes like flame, feet like burnished bronze, voice like many waters.
The great angel stands on sea and land and gives John the little scroll to eat: 'sweet as honey in your mouth, bitter in your stomach.' He must prophesy again.

Dead Sea.region: Lowest point on earth, Jordan rift valley
Dead Sea.desc: The hypersaline lake at the mouth of the Jordan, 430m below sea level — the lowest point on earth. Associated with Sodom's destruction, the Cities of the Plain, and eschatological prophecy.

events.text: The Valley of Siddim (the Dead Sea basin) is the site of the battle of four kings against five, in which Lot is captured and later rescued by Abram.
God rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah in the region now covered by the Dead Sea's S end. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
The Salt Sea (Dead Sea) marks Israel's eastern boundary in Moses's instructions for dividing the land among the tribes.
Ezekiel's eschatological vision: water flows from the Temple eastward into the Dead Sea and heals it — 'the waters become fresh' and fishermen spread nets on its shores.
In the last days, fresh water will flow from Jerusalem to the eastern sea (Dead Sea) and the western sea — the healing of the land made complete.

Mount Hermon.desc: The highest peak in the region (2,814m), capped with snow year-round. Its dew was proverbial for richness; it marks the northern boundary of the Promised Land.

events.text: Moses describes the conquest of Bashan: the Sidonians called Hermon 'Sirion' and the Amorites called it 'Senir' — the great mountain bordering conquered territory.
'Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name' — Hermon as a symbol of the majesty of creation testifying to God's glory.
'Like the dew of Hermon falling on the mountains of Zion' — the unity of brothers compared to Hermon's life-giving dew descending on the covenant community.
The Transfiguration likely occurs on Hermon (or Tabor). Jesus is transformed; Moses and Elijah appear; the Father's voice comes from a bright cloud: 'This is my beloved Son.'
'Come with me from Lebanon, my bride... from the peak of Hermon' — the mountain's majesty as a metaphor for the beloved's splendor.

Sodom.desc: Byword for wickedness throughout Scripture. Destroyed by fire and sulfur, Sodom becomes the Bible's ultimate symbol of divine judgment on unrepentant sin — and a warning to every generation.

events.text: Lot chooses the well-watered Jordan plain and pitches his tent toward Sodom. The narrator notes: 'the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.'
Sodom is attacked by four kings; Lot is taken captive. Abram rescues him with 318 trained men — a small but decisive force.
God reveals to Abraham his plan to destroy Sodom. Abraham intercedes boldly: 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' He negotiates down to ten righteous people.
Only Lot and his two daughters escape. His wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Fire and sulfur rain on the cities of the plain.
Isaiah compares Jerusalem's corrupt leadership to 'rulers of Sodom' — the most devastating possible insult to the holy city.
Jesus says it will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for towns that reject his messengers — ranking the guilt of those with greater revelation.
'Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire' — the paradigm case of judgment.

Dothan.desc: A small town in northern Israel where Joseph was sold into slavery by his brothers and where Elisha's servant saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.

events.text: Joseph finds his brothers at Dothan after they moved from Shechem. They throw him in a pit, then sell him to Ishmaelite traders for 20 shekels of silver.
Elisha is surrounded by an Aramean army at Dothan. His servant is terrified until Elisha prays and the servant sees the hills full of horses and chariots of fire.
Elisha prays that the Aramean soldiers be struck blind, then leads them directly into Samaria, where he prays for their eyes to be opened — and shows them mercy.

Penuel.region: E of Jordan, at the Jabbok River
Penuel.desc: The ford of the Jabbok where Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious opponent — a theophany that transformed him from Jacob ('deceiver') to Israel ('God-wrestler').

events.text: Jacob wrestles alone with a man until daybreak. When the man cannot prevail, he touches Jacob's hip socket and it is put out of joint. Jacob refuses to let go without a blessing.
The man asks Jacob's name, then renames him Israel: 'You have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.' Jacob limps away — forever marked by the encounter.
Gideon threatens the men of Penuel for refusing to feed his army pursuing the Midianite kings. On his return he tears down the city's tower and kills the men.
Hosea recalls Jacob's wrestling at Peniel as a picture of prayer: 'He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor.' An invitation to the same desperate, prevailing prayer.

Gaza.desc: Southern gateway city of Canaan on the coastal trade route. A major Philistine city, where Samson's story ends and from which the Ethiopian treasurer returned home.

events.text: Samson spends the night with a prostitute in Gaza. The Philistines surround the city, but at midnight Samson carries off the city gates to Hebron.
Samson is blinded and imprisoned in Gaza. At the Dagon temple feast he prays one final prayer and pushes down the pillars, killing more than he killed in his life.
An angel directs Philip to go south to 'the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.' There he meets and baptizes the Ethiopian eunuch, who goes on his way rejoicing.
Amos pronounces judgment on Gaza for deporting whole communities to sell them as slaves to Edom — one of the earliest biblical condemnations of the slave trade.

Moab.region: E of the Dead Sea (modern Jordan)
Moab.desc: The plateau east of the Dead Sea, homeland of the Moabites descended from Lot. Israel's penultimate campsite before entering Canaan; Ruth's homeland; David's great-grandmother's country.

events.text: Moab is founded by Lot's son through his elder daughter after the destruction of Sodom — an awkward origin that shaped Israel's ambivalent relationship with Moab.
Balak king of Moab hires Balaam to curse Israel. God turns every curse into a blessing. Balaam's donkey speaks when it sees the angel of the LORD.
Ruth the Moabitess clings to her mother-in-law Naomi: 'Where you go I will go... your God will be my God.' She leaves Moab to return to Bethlehem.
Moses views the Promised Land from Mount Nebo in Moab and dies there. God buries him in Moab; no one knows the place to this day.
Mesha king of Moab rebels against Israel. When his army is surrounded, he offers his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall.

Edom.region: S of the Dead Sea and Dead Sea S (modern S Jordan)
Edom.desc: The rugged, rose-red rock country south of the Dead Sea, homeland of Esau's descendants. Israel and Edom lived in chronic tension; Edom's gloating over Jerusalem's fall made them a target of the prophets.

events.text: Esau settles in the hill country of Seir (Edom) after giving the family land in Canaan to Jacob. His descendants become the Edomite kings.
Moses requests passage through Edom on the way to Canaan: 'Let us pass through your country.' Edom refuses and comes out with a large army. Israel turns away.
The entire book of Obadiah is a single oracle against Edom for standing aside and gloating when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem — 'you should not have gloated over your brother's day.'
The vision of the warrior from Edom with blood-red garments is a picture of divine judgment: 'Who is this who comes from Edom... marching in the greatness of his strength?'
God declares 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' — choosing Israel over Edom — as evidence of his prior sovereign love, regardless of human performance.

Emmaus.desc: The village 7 miles from Jerusalem where two disciples walked with the risen Jesus without recognizing him — until the breaking of bread.

events.text: Two disciples walk from Jerusalem to Emmaus, downcast about the crucifixion. A stranger joins them and explains how the Scriptures required all these things.
'Were not our hearts burning within us while he talked with us on the road?' The stranger breaks bread with them and their eyes are opened. He vanishes.
They rush back to Jerusalem to find the eleven and report: 'The Lord has risen indeed!' — arriving just as Jesus appears in the upper room.

Persia.desc: The world empire that defeated Babylon and released the Jewish exiles. God moved Persian kings to fund the Temple's rebuilding — the largest act of state-sponsored religious restoration in the ancient world.

events.text: Cyrus king of Persia issues his famous edict: 'The LORD... has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem. Whoever is among his people, let him go up.' Fulfilling Isaiah 44:28.
Cyrus's decree is repeated verbatim. The exiles return with 5,400 items of gold and silver taken from the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar.
The story of Esther unfolds in Susa (Shushan), the Persian capital. Haman plots to destroy all the Jews in the empire; Esther risks death to intercede with the king.
Nehemiah is the king's cupbearer in Susa when he hears that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruin. He weeps and prays before asking the king for leave to rebuild.
Daniel has a vision beside the Tigris in Persia. An angel tells him that the 'prince of Persia' (a spiritual power) had resisted Gabriel's coming for 21 days.
